en: Homage to the glorious Khasarpaṇa!

In this place, there was a lay follower (upāsaka) named Śubhaṅkara who performed virtuous deeds and was full of compassion; it is said that he was preparing to go to Potalaka. While traveling, he stayed in a village called Khasarpaṇa located in the district of Khāḍī.
To him, the Blessed One, the Noble Avalokiteśvara, gave this instruction:
"Do not go; remain here with us according to the sequence of the Vairocanābhisambodhi-tantrarāja, for by that a great benefit for sentient beings will come to pass.
Thereupon, he quickly caused the Blessed One to act accordingly;
such is the oral tradition.

In that regard, for the sake of accomplishing the Blessed One’s [path], the perfection of right view is cultivated. For it is said: "O monk, it is better for a monk to have a failure in morality than a failure in view.

Therefore, having first observed all phenomena as momentary and selfless, and being free from all conceptual constructions, one with a compassionate disposition thinks: "Alas! These sentient beings are afflicted by afflictions, karma, and so forth."
Then, being excessively tormented by the sufferings of birth, old age, and death, they experience manifold kinds of suffering; therefore,
having become the Lord of the World (*lokeśvara*), I shall remove their suffering and the like.
"I establish [them] in the wisdom of the omniscient one.

Having thus formed this resolute intention, one should visualize within one's own heart, in the center of a thousand-petaled lotus born from the syllable *paṃ*, upon a moon disc born from the syllable *a*, the five seed-syllables *āṃ tāṃ suṃ bhṛṃ haṃ*.
By means of the garlands of light rays emanating from these, one should summon those Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas so that they appear in the expanse of the sky directly in front.
Having performed the sevenfold worship— consisting of prostration, offering, confession of misdeeds, going for refuge, and so forth— or the elevenfold worship,

one should cultivate the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra) such as loving-kindness and compassion. Then, having uttered, "I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness," and having realized emptiness, the Blessed One Avalokiteśvara becomes the self of the yogin.
And he is white as the autumn moon;
with matted locks forming a crown upon his head, he bears the image of Amitābha and is adorned with all ornaments;
he stands upon a thousand-petaled lotus atop a jeweled lion throne.
Lalitākṣepa has two arms and one face;
he holds a lotus with his left hand and,
with his right, displays the gesture of granting boons while a stream of nectar flows from it.
Seated upon a sattvaparyaṅka,
before him is Tārā, with a complexion like molten gold,
possessing uplifted and full breasts.
Adorned with all ornaments,
her two hands— placed near her eyes like blue lotus buds—
are followed by the youth together with his wealth.
Resplendent with gold,
adorned with jewel ornaments and a jeweled crown, with a lotus fastened under his left arm,
he has joined his palms in reverent salutation.
Following that, she has a frown, wears a crown of matted hair,
is adorned with a *caitya* upon her head,
and is radiant like gold.
Clad in red garments,
she performs a gesture of salutation with her right hand,
while holding a rosary with the other.
With her two left hands she holds a triple staff and a water-pot;
following that is Hayagrīva, blazing and radiant, with tawny hair standing erect,
adorned with snakes, and red in color.
With a protruding belly, clad in a tiger-skin garment,
and holding a staff in his hand—
in this way, the Blessed One, consisting of five aspects, is to be meditated upon.
One who possesses such a retinue should likewise be honored;
this is done once the maṇḍala has been prepared.
There, first having drawn the mandala, one should perform the protection:
*oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi rakṣa o māṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Oṃ vajrarekhe hūṃ. This is the mantra of the maṇḍala.

"Oṃ, come, O Blessed One, to the lion throne in the maṇḍala; oṃ āḥ"—with this mantra, having performed the invitation, one should worship the fivefold [deity] situated upon a thousand-petaled lotus atop the lion throne in the center of the maṇḍala.
Regarding that, the mantra for worship is as follows:
Oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ / Oṃ vajradhūpe hūṃ / Oṃ vajragandhe hūṃ /
Oṃ vajrāloke hūṃ / Oṃ vajrāhāre hūṃ / Having thus performed worship and praise, one should perform the recitation of the mantra.
Oṃ, to the mass of spreading clouds of offerings of all the Tathāgatas, hūṃ! This is the mantra for the consecration of the offerings.
Oṃ āṃ tāṃ suṃ bhṛṃ haṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ, with the beautiful and graceful bows of all the Tathāgatas, I bow to the Blessed One: Jaḥ Hūṃ Vaṃ Hoḥ! Accept this handful of flowers, O Lord, Hoḥ!
This is the mantra of homage.
Oṃ Muḥ Svāhā! This is the mantra of dismissal.
Oṃ kha kha kha hi / Gṛhṇa gṛhṇa gṛhṇantu sarvabhautikā imaṃ baliṃ svāhā / Thus is the mantra for the bali offering.
Then, at the very time of beginning the worship, one should purify the mind by reciting as follows:
"I shall desist from all misdeeds; I shall train myself in the training of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
I shall proceed according to the ritual procedure for worship;
if it were not done in this way,
then the roots of merit would be born of passion, hatred, and delusion.

In this world, all sentient beings indeed possess dispositions of attachment, aversion, and delusion. For instance, by means of a root of virtue born of attachment, there arose the two nāga kings Nanda and Upananda;
by means of aversion born of attachment, [there arose the nāgas]; and by means of delusion born of attachment, the yakṣa Vaiśravaṇa came into being.
Therefore, having abandoned attachment, aversion, delusion, and the like, one should perform all roots of virtue, such as generosity and so forth, with a mind purified by compassion.
Thus ends the *Khasarpaṇasādhana*.
Composed by Śubhaṃkara.
